Multivariate count regression

Source: R/countreg_mv.R
countreg_mv.Rd

Fits several count outcomes observed on the same units, such as crashes by severity or by type at each site, each with its own count family, mean formula and distribution-parameter formulas.

Usage

countreg_mv(
  formula,
  data,
  family = "NB2",
  dis_param_formula_1 = NULL,
  dis_param_formula_2 = NULL,
  offset = NULL,
  weights = NULL,
  group_var = NULL,
  stderr = "normal",
  method = "BFGS",
  max.iters = 1000,
  start.vals = NULL,
  ndraws = 1500,
  engine = "quadrature",
  verbose = FALSE,
  rpar_formula = NULL,
  correlation = c("across", "within", "none"),
  rpar_draws = 500,
  seed = NULL,
  copula = c("none", "gaussian", "frank", "clayton", "gumbel"),
  .setup_only = FALSE
)

Arguments

formula

either a formula with the outcomes on the left as cbind(y_1, ..., y_J) and one right-hand side for every equation, or a list of two-sided formulas, one per outcome (named by the list names, or by their responses). An offset() term (an exposure) belongs in the formulas.

data

a data frame.

family

the count family of each outcome (see count_families): one code for every outcome, or one per outcome (named by outcome or in their order). Families made with new_count_family() are accepted.

dis_param_formula_1, dis_param_formula_2

formulas for the outcomes' distribution parameters, as in countreg(): NULL (constant), one one-sided formula for every outcome that has the parameter, or a list named by outcome (outcomes not in the list keep a constant parameter).

offset

optional names of offset columns (log scale) used by every equation, instead of offset() in the formulas.

weights

optional frequency weights: a column name or a numeric vector.

group_var

optional column naming the units for cluster-robust standard errors (such as a site observed over several years).

stderr

"normal" (from the Hessian, the default), "robust" (sandwich) or "cluster" (sandwich by group_var).

method, max.iters, start.vals, verbose

optimizer settings, as in countreg(); the default method is "BFGS".

ndraws, engine

integration settings of families without a closed form, as in countreg().

rpar_formula

optional one-sided formula of random parameters: one formula for every outcome, or a list named by outcome. Each term adds a normal random deviation, with mean zero, to the coefficient of that variable in the outcome's equation (a variable not in the equation's formula gets a random coefficient with mean zero). The intercept is random only when the formula has the term 1 itself (~ 1, ~ 1 + x). The random parameters are drawn once per unit of group_var (shared by all its rows, such as the years of a site), or once per row without group_var.

correlation

correlation of the random parameters: "across" (default; correlated within and across equations, so the outcomes of a unit share unobserved factors), "within" (correlated within each equation only) or "none".

rpar_draws

the number of simulation draws per unit (randomly shifted Halton points, a separate block and shift for each unit).

seed

seed of the random shifts of the draws (stored in the fit, so predictions use the same draws); random by default.

copula

"none" (default), or a copula that joins the outcomes' distributions: "gaussian" (two outcomes), "frank", "clayton" or "gumbel". See Details.

.setup_only

internal use: return the model setup without fitting.

Value

An object of class "countreg_mv", with methods coef(), vcov(), logLik(), summary(), predict(), fitted(), residuals(), simulate(), tidy(), glance() and confint().

Details

Independent equations. Without rpar_formula, the outcomes are independent given the covariates, so the log-likelihood is the sum of the equations' log-likelihoods and every equation's estimates equal those of a separate countreg() fit. Fitting them together gives one object with joint predictions, simulations and tests across equations (for example, a Wald test that a coefficient is the same in two equations). The rows used are those complete for every equation.

Correlated outcomes. Counts of different categories at a site are usually correlated: unobserved conditions that raise one also raise the others. With rpar_formula, each equation's log mean gets random terms \(x_r' b_{uj}\), with \(b_u = L z_u\) drawn per unit and correlated across equations (correlation = "across").

The multivariate Poisson-lognormal model. Poisson outcomes with correlated normal random intercepts (family = "POISSON", rpar_formula = ~ 1, correlation = "across") give the multivariate Poisson-lognormal model (MVPLN) of, for example, Ma et al. (2008). Other families keep their own overdispersion within each outcome, with the random intercepts adding the correlation between outcomes, and every equation can have a different family. A positive correlation of the random intercepts means that a site with more crashes of one category than its covariates predict also tends to have more of the other. The correlation can be negative too, unlike in models with a shared gamma effect such as negmultinom(). The likelihood is simulated (rpar_draws draws per unit) with analytic gradients; the elements of \(L\) are reported as sd: and chol:, and summary() shows the implied standard deviations and correlations. predict() gives joint and conditional probabilities of the outcomes, and Empirical Bayes predictions for units in the estimation data.

Copulas. A copula joins the outcomes' own distributions, each with its family, into one joint distribution: \(P(Y_1 \le y_1, \dots, Y_J \le y_J) = C(F_1(y_1), \dots, F_J(y_J); \theta)\). For counts, the probability of the observed combination is the exact volume of the copula over the rectangle \([F_j(y_j - 1), F_j(y_j)]\) (the sum over its \(2^J\) corners; Nikoloulopoulos and Karlis 2009), not a continuous approximation such as the midpoint or jittering. The margins are those of the equations, so expected counts and each outcome's probabilities do not change; the copula changes the joint and conditional probabilities. The families differ in the shape of the dependence:

  • "gaussian": symmetric, without tail dependence, any sign (copula:atanh(rho)); two outcomes.

  • "frank": symmetric, without tail dependence; any sign for two outcomes (copula:theta), positive for more (copula:ln(theta)).

  • "clayton": positive, stronger in the lower tail (joint low counts; copula:ln(theta)).

  • "gumbel": positive, stronger in the upper tail (joint high counts; copula:ln(theta - 1)).

All parameters are estimated together by maximum likelihood, started from the separate equations and the copula parameter that is best for them (inference functions for margins). summary() reports the copula parameter and its Kendall's tau. With counts, the copula is not unique outside the range of the margins (Genest and Neslehova 2007): its parameter describes this model's dependence, and the tau is that of the copula, not the rank correlation of the counts, which is weaker for small counts. The gradient is analytic: the derivatives of the copula and of each outcome's distribution function, \(\partial F(y) / \partial \theta = \sum_{k \le y} f(k)\, \partial \log f(k) / \partial \theta\).

Copulas with random parameters. copula and rpar_formula can be combined: given a unit's random parameters, the outcomes of each row are joined by the copula, and the unit's likelihood averages over the random parameters. The random parameters, shared by the rows of a unit (such as the years of a site), carry the dependence between units' outcomes over time; the copula carries the dependence that remains within each row.

Different outcomes often need different families: frequent property damage crashes may be close to NB2, while rare fatal crashes are more skewed and zero-heavy. Each equation can use any family of the package.

References

Genest, C., and Neslehova, J. (2007). A primer on copulas for count data. ASTIN Bulletin, 37(2), 475-515.

Ma, J., Kockelman, K. M., and Damien, P. (2008). A multivariate Poisson-lognormal regression model for prediction of crash counts by severity, using Bayesian methods. Accident Analysis and Prevention, 40(3), 964-975.

Nikoloulopoulos, A. K., and Karlis, D. (2009). Modeling multivariate count data using copulas. Communications in Statistics - Simulation and Computation, 39(1), 172-187.

See also

predict.countreg_mv(), countreg(), countreg_alloc() for a total and its split across categories, negmultinom()

Examples

# \donttest{
data("washington_roads")
w <- washington_roads
w$pdo <- w$Total_crashes - w$Injury_crashes
m <- countreg_mv(cbind(pdo, Injury_crashes) ~ lnaadt + speed50 +
                   offset(lnlength), data = w,
                 family = c(pdo = "NB2", Injury_crashes = "PIG"))
summary(m)
#> Multivariate count model

#> Std. errors: normal

#>

#>             Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)
